feedback: If a learner guesses the group before answering the questions: 'Answer the feature questions first — the key decides the group for you.'
When the key narrows correctly: 'Notice which single feature answer settled it — that's the defining feature of the group.'
If a learner gets stuck on a near-miss: 'Go back one step. Which feature answer did you give? Check it against the real animal.'
For the 'why it helps' step: 'A rainforest has thousands of species — a shared feature-key lets scientists sort and study that huge variety in an organised way.'
activities.intendedInsight: A classification key makes sorting criterion-driven, reversible and checkable: each feature question narrows the possibilities until one group remains, so the answer is justified by features rather than by a lucky guess.
learnerActions: Use a branching yes/no key that asks about one feature at a time: 'Does it make its own food (a plant)?' → 'Does it have feathers?' → 'Does it have fur / feed milk?' → 'Does it have dry scales?' → 'Does it have moist, smooth skin with no scales?' → 'Six legs and three body parts?' — each 'yes' leads to one of the six groups (an organism that answers 'no' to every question, such as a spider or worm, belongs to a different group).
Run a tricky animal (e.g. the bat) through the key: answer 'feathers? no … fur? yes … feeds milk? yes' and watch the key narrow to MAMMAL.
Run at least two more organisms (e.g. caiman, tree frog, leaf-cutter ant) through the key and record which feature answer settled the group.
Reverse the process: pick a group and name the sequence of feature answers that leads to it, checking the key is reversible.
Discuss: because each step tests a feature, the group is decided by the criterion, not by a guess.
activities.title: Branching yes/no key: let the criterion decide

feedback: Gap response (sorts by behaviour/habitat, can't name a feature): reteach observable body features — fur+milk means mammal regardless of flying — before re-attempting.
Partial (sorts most but slips on bat/caiman or can't state the rule): revisit the branching key on just the tricky cases and name the deciding feature.
Full (sorts eight+, states each defining feature, applies rule to a tricky/new case): extend to justifying WHY a bat or tree frog belongs in its group and why classification helps scientists.

On the bat question: 'No — the macaw is a bird but the bat is a mammal. Group by body features, not by what they do: birds have feathers, wings, beaks and lay eggs; the bat has fur and feeds milk, so it is a mammal even though it flies.'

On the fur-that-lays-eggs case: use the key and observable features — fur (hair) and feeding milk are the mammal features, and ALL mammals feed their young milk, even the few that lay eggs. So an animal with fur that lays eggs, like the platypus or echidna, is still a mammal; laying eggs is an unusual exception, not a reason to change its group.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who has met the objective sorts by observable features, states the defining feature for each group, and applies the feature-rule correctly to tricky or novel cases — not by what an animal does or where it lives.
learnerActions: Sort at least eight rainforest organisms into their correct groups (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, insects, plants).
For each group, state the key feature that defines it (e.g. 'mammals have fur and feed milk to their young').
Answer the diagnostic: 'A bat flies by night, a macaw flies by day; both have wings and fly — are they both birds? Put each into its group and explain WHY.'
Explain in your own words why sorting living things into groups helps scientists understand and study the huge variety of rainforest life.
Apply the rule to a NEW or tricky case: 'If you found an animal with fur that lays eggs, how would you decide its group?'
activities.title: Classification check: sort and justify
